theme: Trust only what you can verify

questions.concept: Prioritising frame rate over resolution for sign-language video calls
questions.question: You're the PM for a video-calling app. Deaf users who sign say calls are 'unusable' on mid-range mobile networks, even though audio-first users rate call quality highly on the same networks. The adaptive video system currently keeps resolution high and drops frames when bandwidth falls. What is the best first change?
options: A 'signing mode' that holds a high, steady frame rate and lowers background resolution when bandwidth drops
Automatic live captions on every call so deaf users can read along while the video is choppy
A higher default video resolution for all calls so that hand shapes appear sharper on screen
A prompt asking deaf users to switch to Wi-Fi before they start a call on a mobile network
rationales: Correct: it changes the trade-off the system makes so that motion, which carries meaning in sign language, is protected first.
Captions transcribe speech, not signing, so they don't help two signers talking to each other.
Higher resolution uses more bandwidth, which makes frame drops worse on the very networks causing the problem.
This puts the burden on users and ignores that the system's trade-off is wrong for their use case; many won't have Wi-Fi.
questions.explanation: In sign language the meaning is carried by motion: hand shapes, transitions and facial expressions. The current system was tuned for speakers, where a sharp but jerky picture is fine because the audio carries the content. Dropped frames delete parts of signs, so for signers smooth motion matters more than detail. Re-weighting the trade-off for this use case fixes the actual failure.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers reward candidates who ask what the user's content is carried by. A strong answer shows the existing design embeds an assumption from the majority use case and re-tunes it, rather than bolting on features.

questions.concept: Doctor-approved visit summary in the patient's language
questions.question: A telemedicine app in India finds that about a third of patients call the clinic within 48 hours of a consultation to ask what the doctor said about dosage and follow-up. Most consultations are in English, but many of these patients prefer Hindi or Tamil. What should you build first?
options: An in-app chat channel so patients can message the doctor with questions after the visit
An auto-generated visit summary in the patient's chosen language, approved by the doctor before it is sent
Medication reminders sent as push notifications at the times the doctor recommended
A recording of the full consultation that patients can replay at any time from their visit history
rationales: Chat moves the same questions onto doctors' time and may increase contacts rather than reduce them.
Correct: it targets the cause (comprehension and recall in a second language) with a short, trusted artefact.
Reminders assume the patient already understands the dosage; they don't fix the misunderstanding.
A replay is long, still in English, and hard to search for the one dosage detail the patient needs.
questions.explanation: The repeat calls come from patients not understanding or remembering instructions, made worse by a language gap. A short summary of dosage and next steps in the patient's own language solves both at the moment they need it, and doctor approval keeps it safe. It also removes the calls rather than moving them to another channel.
questions.interview_tip: Strong answers trace a support symptom (repeat calls) back to the root need and solve it where it starts. Mentioning the safety check on medical content shows judgment.

questions.concept: Matching recurring carpools on schedule reliability over route fit
questions.question: You launched an office carpool feature for a large Bengaluru tech park. Riders who are matched once rarely ride again. The top reason in exit surveys is 'the driver's leaving time kept changing'. Which change to matching would most improve repeat rides?
options: Give riders cashback on their second ride so they have a reason to try the service again
Match riders with drivers who need the smallest detour, so that every single ride is as quick as possible
Match riders with drivers whose past departure times have been consistent, weighting reliability above route overlap
Let riders rate drivers after every trip and show the average rating on the match screen
rationales: An incentive may buy one more ride, but riders will leave again when timing stays unreliable.
Smaller detours improve a single trip but don't fix the unpredictable timing that drives churn.
Correct: it builds the user's main need, a predictable departure time, into who gets matched.
Ratings are slow and general; they don't specifically predict whether a driver keeps a schedule.
questions.explanation: Commuters need to plan their day around a fixed time, so predictability is the core value of a carpool. The matching algorithm optimised for route fit, which matters less than whether the driver leaves when expected. Using drivers' history of consistent departures as a matching signal directly addresses the stated churn reason.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers look for whether you connect the stated churn reason to the system's objective function. Naming what the algorithm optimises, and changing it, is a strong signal.

questions.concept: Verifiable part-replacement evidence for doorstep repair services
questions.question: A doorstep two-wheeler repair marketplace gets plenty of first bookings but few repeat bookings. In interviews, customers say they suspect mechanics charge for parts they never replaced, but they rarely dispute bills because they can't prove anything. What should you build first?
options: A detailed itemised invoice emailed to the customer automatically after every completed service
A 10% discount on the second booking to give first-time customers a reason to come back
Photos of each replaced part before and after, the old part handed back, and prices checked against a published parts list
A star rating for each mechanic shown on the booking page so customers can pick trusted mechanics
rationales: An invoice is still the mechanic's own claim; listing a part doesn't prove it was replaced.
A discount doesn't change the suspicion; customers who feel cheated won't return for a small saving.
Correct: it gives customers proof they can verify, which removes the suspicion behind low repeat rates.
Customers can't rate what they can't see, so ratings won't capture hidden over-billing.
questions.explanation: The problem is information asymmetry: the customer can't see what was done, so they assume the worst and don't return. The fix is evidence the customer can check themselves — the old part, photos and a standard price. This turns a 'trust me' claim into something verifiable and also discourages over-billing.
questions.interview_tip: In product-sense rounds, spotting information asymmetry and designing verification is a strong move. Explain why generic trust features (ratings, invoices) fail when the customer can't observe the work.

questions.concept: Email security scanners auto-clicking links inflate verification rates
questions.question: A B2B SaaS product added email verification to signup. For signups from company email domains, the verification rate jumped from 62% to 97% within a week, but activation (first project created) for those users didn't change. For Gmail signups, verification stayed at 64%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Company email security scanners open the verification link automatically, so 'verified' no longer means a person clicked
The new flow made verifying easier for everyone, and company users simply benefited from it more
Company users are more motivated than Gmail users, so nearly all of them verify their email right away
Single sign-on is creating duplicate company accounts, so each company signup is counted twice
rationales: Correct: it explains why only company domains jumped, why the rise was sudden, and why downstream behaviour didn't move.
If the flow helped everyone, Gmail signups would have improved as well, but they stayed flat.
Motivation would show up in activation too, and it wouldn't change overnight to 97%.
Duplicate accounts would inflate signup counts, not push the share of verified signups close to 100%.
questions.explanation: Many corporate mail systems scan links in incoming email by fetching them, which triggers a verification link built as a simple GET request. That explains a sudden near-100% rate only for company domains, with no change in activation. The fix is a landing page where the user must click a button (a POST) to confirm.
questions.interview_tip: In root-cause questions, a jump that's too clean in one segment with no downstream effect usually points to measurement. Strong candidates check whether the event still means what they think it means.

questions.concept: Volume-weighted MAPE for forecasts with many low-volume items
questions.question: A quick-commerce PM tracks demand-forecast accuracy as MAPE averaged across all SKUs. It shows a poor 85% error, yet top sellers rarely stock out. Most of the error comes from SKUs that sell 0–2 units a day, where being off by one unit is a 50–100% error. What is the better headline metric?
options: Plain MAPE after removing every SKU that sells fewer than five units a day from the calculation
Volume-weighted MAPE (total absolute error divided by total units), with slow movers tracked separately
Average forecast bias, because over-forecasts and under-forecasts should cancel each other out
The share of SKUs whose forecast exactly matched the units sold on a given day
rationales: Removing slow movers hides real availability problems on those items instead of measuring them properly.
Correct: weighting by volume makes the metric reflect operational impact while keeping slow movers visible separately.
Bias shows direction, not size; large errors in both directions can cancel to look perfect.
Exact matches are rare for any item with variable demand, so this metric is noisy and not very useful.
questions.explanation: Simple MAPE gives every SKU equal weight, so tiny-volume items with huge percentage errors dominate the average. Weighting by volume (often called WAPE) reflects errors in proportion to the units that matter for operations. Slow movers still need watching, so track them with their own metric instead of letting them swamp the headline.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who check how a metric is aggregated before trusting it. Pointing out equal weighting across very different units shows analytical maturity.

questions.concept: North Star for a home-services marketplace
questions.question: You're setting the North Star for a home-services marketplace (plumbers, electricians, cleaners). Leadership proposes 'bookings per week'. Which North Star better reflects value for both customers and professionals?
options: Number of service professionals active on the platform each week
Gross booking value per week across all service categories
Jobs completed per week with no rework or complaint within seven days
Average customer star rating across all jobs completed that week
rationales: Supply is an input, not the outcome; professionals can be active without customers getting good service.
Booking value can rise from price increases or cancelled jobs and says nothing about whether work was done well.
Correct: it measures delivered value to both sides and includes quality, not just activity.
Ratings are a quality signal, but they don't grow with volume and suffer from rating inflation.
questions.explanation: A booking is only an intent; value is delivered when the job is done well. Counting completed jobs without rework captures the customer's outcome and the professional's paid work at once, and it penalises cancellations and poor quality that 'bookings' ignores. It still grows with volume, so it works as a growth target.
questions.interview_tip: A strong North Star answer explains why the obvious activity metric falls short and picks the moment value is actually delivered to both sides.

questions.concept: ARPA calculation versus revenue per seat
questions.question: A B2B SaaS company has 400 paying accounts, 6,000 paid seats and $2.4M in monthly recurring revenue. What is its monthly ARPA (average revenue per account)?
rationales: This is revenue per seat ($2.4M ÷ 6,000 seats), not per account.
This confuses units; it doesn't come from dividing revenue by accounts.
This divides seats by accounts (15 seats each) and mixes it up with revenue.
questions.explanation: ARPA divides recurring revenue by the number of paying accounts: $2.4M ÷ 400 = $6,000 per account per month. Revenue per seat is a different metric ($2.4M ÷ 6,000 = $400). Tracking both helps separate whether growth comes from more seats per account or higher prices.
questions.interview_tip: Quick metric definitions come up as warm-ups. Getting the denominator right, and explaining why ARPA and per-seat revenue tell different stories, shows fluency.

questions.concept: Central limit theorem justifies t-tests on skewed metrics at large samples
questions.question: You're testing a change on revenue per user. About 95% of users spend nothing and a few spend a lot. You have 400,000 users per arm. An analyst says a t-test is invalid because revenue isn't normally distributed. What's the correct response?
options: Log-transform revenue and report the lift in mean log revenue as the revenue lift
Drop users with zero revenue so that the remaining revenue values look closer to normal
Use a Mann-Whitney test instead, because it compares the two means without assuming normality
With samples this large, the mean is approximately normal, so a t-test on the mean is valid; heavy tails mainly widen the interval
rationales: A lift in mean log revenue is not a lift in mean revenue, and log of zero is undefined for most users.
Dropping zeros conditions on buying, which the treatment may change, and changes what you're measuring.
Mann-Whitney compares rank distributions, not means, so it answers a different question than revenue lift.
Correct: it applies the central limit theorem correctly and keeps the metric the business cares about (mean revenue).
questions.explanation: The t-test needs the sampling distribution of the mean to be roughly normal, not the raw data. With hundreds of thousands of users, the central limit theorem gives that even for skewed data. Heavy tails make the variance larger, which you can handle with more data, capping extreme values or variance reduction.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers test whether you know which assumption a test actually needs. A strong answer separates 'data is skewed' from 'the estimate is unreliable' and mentions practical fixes for variance.

questions.concept: Choosing qualitative validation and staged rollout when an A/B test can't be powered
questions.question: You're the PM at a B2B SaaS company with 120 enterprise customers. You've redesigned the admin console. A power calculation says you'd need about 3,000 accounts per arm to detect a 5% change in admin task completion. What's the best approach?
options: Run the A/B test anyway for a full quarter so that enough data builds up to reach significance
Randomise at the user level instead of the account level so there are more units in each arm
Skip the A/B test; run usability sessions with admins, then a staged rollout with before-and-after tracking and feedback
Run the test with a looser significance threshold, such as p < 0.30, so a result is more likely to appear
rationales: Running longer doesn't add accounts; the number of customers, not the days, limits power here.
Admins in the same company would see different consoles, causing confusion and contamination, and there are still few admins.
Correct: it uses methods that work with small samples and still reduces risk through staging.
A loose threshold just raises false positives; it doesn't make the test informative.
questions.explanation: With 120 accounts, no amount of waiting gets you to 3,000 per arm, so a test would be badly underpowered and its result misleading. Better evidence comes from watching admins use the console and from a careful staged rollout with clear signals and a way back. Choosing the right method for the sample you have is part of good experimentation.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who know when not to A/B test. A strong answer quantifies why the test can't work and offers a credible alternative that still manages risk.

questions.concept: Monthly pet-grooming appointments in Bengaluru
questions.question: Estimate the number of paid pet-grooming appointments (salon or at-home) in Bengaluru per month.
options: About 40,000
About 40 lakh
About 4 lakh
About 4,000
rationales: Correct: households × dog ownership × paid-grooming share × frequency gives about 40,000.
This is more appointments than there are dogs in the city each month, which is impossible.
This would need every pet dog groomed more than once a month, which is far above typical frequency.
This would mean only about 8,000 regularly groomed dogs in a city of 35 lakh households, which is too low.
questions.explanation: Bengaluru has about 1.4 crore people, roughly 35 lakh households. If about 8% own a dog, that's around 2.8 lakh dogs (cats rarely use paid grooming). Perhaps 30% of those owners pay for grooming, giving about 85,000 dogs, groomed about once every two months: 85,000 ÷ 2 ≈ 40,000 appointments a month.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers care about a clear chain: population → households → ownership → usage → frequency. State each assumption out loud and sanity-check the result against the number of dogs.

questions.concept: Annual new driving licences issued in India
questions.question: Estimate roughly how many new driving licences are issued in India each year.
options: About 15 lakh
About 1.5 lakh
About 1.5 crore
About 15 crore
rationales: This would mean only about 6% of young adults get licensed, which is too low for a country with so many two-wheelers.
This would mean less than 1% of each age group ever gets a licence, which ignores India's huge two-wheeler use.
Correct: about 2.4 crore people turning 18 × roughly half getting licences, plus late applicants, gives about 1.5 crore.
This is more than the entire age group turning 18 every year, so it can't be right.
questions.explanation: India has about 145 crore people, so roughly 2.4 crore people turn 18 each year. If around half of each age group gets a licence over time (mostly for two-wheelers), that's about 1.2 crore, plus some older first-time applicants, giving about 1.5 crore a year. The method matters more than the exact number.
questions.interview_tip: Start from the flow of people entering the eligible age group. A quick upper-bound check (no more than the yearly cohort plus catch-up) shows good estimation habits.

questions.concept: Embedded distribution of insurance at the point of purchase
questions.question: A travel-insurance startup spends ₹900 on search ads to acquire each customer, but the average premium is ₹600. Which go-to-market move would most improve its unit economics?
options: Run a brand-awareness TV campaign to lower acquisition costs over the next few years
Cut the premium so the policy is the cheapest option shown in search results
Add more coverage options so that customers buy higher-priced plans on average
Offer the policy as an add-on inside airline and travel-booking checkouts, paying partners a revenue share
rationales: TV is expensive and slow, and insurance bought at booking time doesn't gain much from general awareness.
Lower prices cut revenue per customer while ad costs stay the same, making the gap worse.
Bigger plans may raise revenue a little, but they don't fix paying more to acquire a customer than they bring in.
Correct: it reaches customers at the point of need and makes acquisition cost a share of revenue.
questions.explanation: Travel insurance is bought at the moment of booking, and booking sites already have that customer's attention. Embedding the policy in their checkout reaches high-intent buyers at a cost tied to sales (a revenue share) rather than paying for clicks up front. This is why embedded insurance is a common distribution model.
questions.interview_tip: In strategy rounds, show that you can find where customers already are when they need the product. Talking about partner incentives and revenue share shows business depth.

questions.concept: Creating a new category when buyers anchor on an incumbent's
questions.question: Your startup's product lets finance teams close their books continuously instead of in a monthly rush. Buyers keep comparing it to cheaper 'close checklist' tools with longer feature lists, and you lose those comparisons. What is the most defensible positioning choice?
options: Define a new category around the outcome (a continuous close), target teams who feel month-end pain most, and accept a longer sales cycle
Match the checklist tools' feature lists so that you win the side-by-side feature comparisons
Position as the best checklist tool and mention continuous closing as an extra feature
Price below the checklist tools so buyers see you as the better deal in the comparison
rationales: Correct: it changes the basis of comparison to your strength and names the costs of doing so.
Copying features plays the incumbents' game and drains resources from your real difference.
Calling yourself a checklist tool invites the very comparison you lose and hides your main advantage.
A lower price in the old category suggests a lesser product and lowers margins without changing the frame.
questions.explanation: If buyers put you in an existing category, they judge you by its rules — features and price — where the incumbents win. A product that changes how the work is done is better framed as a new category, defined by the outcome it delivers. That takes education and a longer sales cycle, so it works best when you start with the buyers who feel the pain most.
questions.interview_tip: Strong strategy answers notice when the battle is about the frame, not the features. Naming the cost of category creation (education, sales cycle) shows balanced judgment.

questions.concept: Tiered loyalty status as a forward-looking switching cost
questions.question: Why do airline status tiers (for example, Gold after a certain number of miles a year) keep frequent flyers loyal even though they have no contract?
options: Frequent flyers have higher incomes, so they care less about the price of each ticket
Status members pay an annual membership fee that they would lose by switching airlines
Airline miles legally cannot be moved to other airlines, so travellers are forced to stay
Status earned now carries benefits into future years, so moving spend to a rival means giving up progress and perks
rationales: Income may reduce price sensitivity, but it doesn't explain loyalty to one airline in particular.
Most airline status tiers are earned by flying, not bought with an annual fee.
Miles can't usually be transferred, but that's about point balances, not why tiers increase loyalty.
Correct: the switching cost is the progress and future perks you'd give up.
questions.explanation: Tier programmes make benefits depend on how much you've already flown with the airline. Each new flight builds progress toward future perks, so switching resets that progress. This creates a switching cost that grows with loyalty, without any contract.
questions.interview_tip: When discussing moats, show you can name how a switching cost is created. Loyalty tiers are a simple example of costs that rise the more a customer uses you.

questions.concept: Writing acceptance criteria for an AI feature as eval thresholds
questions.question: Your team is shipping an AI feature that drafts replies to customer emails. Engineering asks for acceptance criteria. Which is the best way to write them?
options: On a fixed set of 300 real emails, at least 90% of drafts are rated 'send with minor edits or better', with zero policy violations on a safety set
Given a refund request email, the draft reply must match the approved template reply word for word
The feature is done when the model returns a draft for every incoming email without errors
Drafts must be helpful, accurate and on-brand for every type of customer email we receive
rationales: Correct: it is measurable, uses real data, and sets different bars for quality and safety.
Word-for-word matching fails good drafts that are worded differently; AI outputs aren't deterministic.
This only checks that the system runs, not whether the drafts are any good.
These words are goals, not criteria; nobody can test whether they've been met.
questions.explanation: AI outputs vary, so acceptance criteria should be thresholds on an agreed eval set rather than exact outputs. A pass rate on representative examples, plus a strict bar on safety, makes 'done' measurable and testable. It also gives a baseline to catch regressions later.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews often ask how you define 'done' for a probabilistic feature. Answering with an eval set, a threshold and a safety bar shows you can manage AI delivery.

questions.concept: Hypercare period after enterprise go-live
questions.question: Your company plans a 'hypercare' period after an enterprise customer goes live on your platform. What does this mean?
options: A premium support plan that is sold to customers as a paid add-on
A code freeze that blocks every release to that customer for the first quarter
An extended free trial given before the customer signs the full contract
A set window right after go-live with closer monitoring, faster support and a direct line to the product team
rationales: It is usually part of the rollout plan, not a separately sold support tier.
Hypercare is about support and monitoring, not stopping releases, though teams may release more carefully.
A trial happens before purchase; hypercare happens after the customer is live.
Correct: it is a time-limited period of extra support right after go-live.
questions.explanation: The first weeks after go-live are when problems are most likely and most damaging to the relationship. Hypercare means extra attention for a fixed time: closer monitoring, faster responses and quick access to the people who can fix things. It ends with a handover to normal support.
questions.interview_tip: B2B execution questions check whether you think beyond launch day. Mentioning hypercare and a clear exit to normal support shows you own the customer outcome.

questions.concept: Archiving stale backlog items (backlog bankruptcy)
questions.question: Your backlog has 1,400 tickets, most over a year old, and grooming meetings waste hours on items nobody will build. What is the most practical fix?
options: Sort the backlog by creation date and build the oldest tickets first
Hire a project manager to look after the backlog full-time going forward
Hold a team offsite to re-estimate and re-rank every ticket in the backlog
Archive tickets untouched for six months or more, with a note; anything important will come up again
rationales: Age is not value; the oldest tickets are often the least relevant now.
Adding a person to manage clutter keeps the clutter; the problem is what's in the backlog.
Re-estimating 1,400 mostly irrelevant items wastes far more time than it saves.
Correct: it removes noise cheaply, and nothing is lost because archived items can be restored.
questions.explanation: A huge backlog of old tickets hides the work that matters and costs time to manage. Archiving stale items, sometimes called backlog bankruptcy, is cheap and safe: real needs come back through customers or the team. The backlog then stays a short list of real options.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like PMs who keep process light. Showing you'd cut waste instead of adding more process signals good judgment.

questions.concept: Weighing a single evidence-backed dissent in a hiring debrief
questions.question: In a debrief for a senior PM candidate, five interviewers say 'strong hire'. One junior interviewer says 'no hire', noting the candidate twice brushed off an engineer's questions and took credit for team results. The hiring manager wants to move on. You're the most senior interviewer. What do you do?
options: Ask for another interview round so the candidate can respond to the concern
Ask the dissenter for the specific evidence, check if others saw related signals, and decide on evidence, not vote count
Go with the majority, since five strong-hire votes clearly outweigh one no-hire vote
Recommend no-hire, since a single no-hire vote should block any senior hire
rationales: Another round may help only if the evidence stays unclear; doing it first avoids the hard discussion.
Correct: it treats the dissent as data, tests it, and decides on the evidence.
Majority voting ignores the content of the concern and may be swayed by seniority and momentum.
An automatic veto ignores whether the concern is well supported; it still needs examining.
questions.explanation: Hiring decisions should rest on evidence, not on counting votes. The dissent names specific, relevant behaviour (how the candidate treats others and credits the team) that the others may not have tested. Drawing it out and checking it against other interviewers' notes protects the bar and makes the decision fair to the candidate.
questions.interview_tip: Bar-raiser style questions test whether you can slow a group down when evidence calls for it. Strong answers show respect for junior voices and a decision process based on evidence.

questions.concept: Responding to team questions about rumoured layoffs without breaking confidence
questions.question: Layoff rumours are spreading. An engineer on your team asks you directly if your team is affected. You've been told in confidence that a reorg is being discussed, but nothing has been decided. What is the best response?
options: Say you can't share everything you hear, that you know of no decision affecting the team, and that you'll tell them what you can as soon as you can
Tell them about the reorg discussion so they can prepare, and ask them to keep it quiet
Reassure them firmly that there will be no layoffs on your team so they can stay focused
Say you haven't heard anything at all, so the rumour loses steam on your team
rationales: Correct: it is honest, keeps the confidence, and avoids a promise you can't guarantee.
Sharing confidential plans breaks trust with leadership and spreads anxiety about something undecided.
You don't control the outcome, so a firm promise could become a broken one and destroy trust.
This is a lie; if the reorg happens, the team will learn you knew and stop trusting you.
questions.explanation: You need to be honest without breaking a confidence or making promises you can't keep. Saying there are limits to what you can share, stating what is true now, and committing to update them keeps trust. Pointing people to what they can control also helps reduce anxiety.
questions.interview_tip: Leadership questions about uncertain news test integrity under pressure. A strong answer balances honesty, confidentiality and care for the team without false comfort.

questions.concept: Recommending a wind-down of the product you were hired to grow
questions.question: You were hired to grow a product line. After six weeks of analysis, you believe it should be wound down: the market is shrinking, and the team could create more value elsewhere. Your VP championed the product. What should you do?
options: Present the analysis with options (wind down, reposition, maintain) and a recommendation, including what the freed team could do next
Spend a year trying to grow it first, so you've earned credibility before raising any concerns
Tell the team first that the product will probably be shut down so they can plan ahead
Quietly move the product to maintenance mode and shift the team's effort without discussing it
rationales: Correct: it is candid, evidence-based, gives the decision-maker options, and shows the opportunity cost.
Waiting a year wastes resources on a path you believe is wrong; credibility comes from good judgment, not delay.
Telling the team before the decision is made creates anxiety and undercuts the VP's role.
Changing direction without discussion goes around your VP and breaks trust.
questions.explanation: Your job is to make the best call for the company, even if it's not what you were hired to do. A clear analysis with options respects the VP's investment, gives them a real choice, and shows the upside of moving the team. Raising it early saves a year of wasted effort.
questions.interview_tip: This tests Amazon-style 'Are Right, A Lot' and 'Have Backbone'. Strong answers show you can disagree with the premise of your own role while managing the stakeholder carefully.

questions.concept: Preserving table headers when chunking documents for RAG
questions.question: An internal RAG assistant answers questions from HR policy PDFs. It handles prose questions well but often gets leave-entitlement questions wrong. These answers live in large tables (grade × location × leave type). Traces show the retrieved chunks contain table rows without their column headers. What's the best fix?
options: Add worked examples of leave questions and answers to the assistant's system prompt
Parse tables separately so each chunk keeps its row and column headers, or store them as structured data
Increase the chunk size so that whole pages of the PDFs are embedded as single chunks
Switch to a larger generation model with stronger reasoning to interpret the table rows
rationales: Examples don't put the missing headers back into the retrieved text, so answers stay unreliable.
Correct: it fixes the root cause shown in the traces — chunks losing the context that gives the numbers meaning.
Large tables still get split across chunks, and bigger chunks dilute retrieval for every other question.
No model can reliably infer which column a number belongs to when the headers are missing.
questions.explanation: A table row without headers is just a list of numbers; neither retrieval nor the model can tell what they mean. Handling tables separately so each chunk carries its headers (or querying them as structured data) gives the model the context it needs. The traces point to a retrieval-input problem, not a generation problem.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers reward candidates who diagnose from traces before choosing a fix. Saying 'the problem is in what we retrieve, not how the model reasons' shows strong AI product instincts.

questions.concept: Policy adherence decaying over long multi-turn conversations
questions.question: A banking assistant's system prompt says 'never give personal investment recommendations'. Single-turn evals pass 100%. But in production, most violations happen after 25+ turns, as users slowly steer the conversation toward stock picks. What should the PM prioritise?
options: Fine-tune the model on more single-turn examples of refusing investment questions
Add long, multi-turn adversarial conversations to the eval set and check every response with a separate policy classifier
Repeat the rule three times in the system prompt so the model remembers it better
Cap conversations at 20 turns and ask users to start a fresh chat after that
rationales: Single-turn training data doesn't teach the model to hold firm under slow, multi-turn pressure.
Correct: it closes the eval gap and adds a layer of protection that doesn't weaken with conversation length.
Repeating the rule may help a little, but it's unmeasured and still relies on the model alone.
A turn cap hurts genuine long conversations, and determined users can simply start over.
questions.explanation: The eval set doesn't contain the situation where failures happen, so it gives false confidence. Long conversations where users push slowly are a known way models drift from instructions. The PM should make the eval represent this pattern and add a check on every turn that doesn't depend on the model remembering its instructions.
questions.interview_tip: Strong AI PM answers notice when evals don't match production conditions. Pairing better evals with a defence that doesn't depend on the model is a good signal.

questions.concept: MCP vs Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol roles
questions.question: Your team is connecting an AI assistant to other systems. What is the main difference between the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol?
options: MCP runs only on the user's device, while A2A runs only on cloud servers
MCP is designed for text-based models, while A2A is designed for voice-based agents
MCP connects an agent to tools and data sources; A2A lets separate agents find each other and hand off tasks
A2A is the newer version of MCP and replaces it for all new integrations
rationales: Both can run locally or remotely; deployment location is not the difference.
Neither protocol is tied to text or voice; both are about how systems connect.
Correct: MCP is agent-to-tool; A2A is agent-to-agent.
They address different layers and are complementary; A2A doesn't replace MCP.
questions.explanation: MCP standardises how an AI application calls tools and reads data, such as a database or file store. A2A, introduced by Google in 2025, standardises how independent agents describe what they can do and delegate tasks to each other. They solve different problems and are often used together.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews increasingly check vocabulary for agent systems. Explaining which problem each protocol solves shows technical fluency.

questions.concept: Handling multi-intent messages in a support bot
questions.question: A telecom support bot assigns one intent to each message. 18% of first messages contain two requests (e.g., 'my bill is wrong, and I also want to port my number'). These conversations escalate twice as often, usually because the second request is ignored. What's the best fix?
options: Detect messages with more than one request, confirm both with the user, and handle them in turn, tracking each to resolution
Add a combined 'billing and porting' intent for the most common pair of requests
Tell users in the greeting to send only one request per message to the bot
Send every message with more than one request straight to a human agent
rationales: Correct: it changes the bot to match how users actually write and makes each request trackable.
Combined intents don't scale: there are too many possible pairs, and the logic still handles them as one.
Users mostly ignore instructions like this, and it pushes the burden onto them.
Many of these requests could be handled automatically; routing all of them wastes human time.
questions.explanation: The bot's design assumes one intent per message, which doesn't match how people write. Detecting and splitting the requests, confirming them and handling each in turn fixes the cause of escalations. Measuring resolution per request also makes the failure visible.
questions.interview_tip: Strong answers notice a design assumption that doesn't match user behaviour, then fix the system rather than asking users to adapt.

questions.concept: Enforcing a terminology glossary in LLM translation
questions.question: An e-commerce company uses an LLM to translate product listings into Hindi, Tamil and Bengali. Sellers complain that brand names and terms like 'cashback' are translated differently from one listing to the next. What's the simplest effective fix?
options: Ask sellers to write their own listings in every language they want to sell in
Give the model a glossary of terms to keep or translate a set way, and check outputs against it automatically
Raise the sampling temperature so the model picks more natural-sounding words
Switch to word-by-word dictionary translation so the output stays accurate
rationales: This pushes the work onto sellers and defeats the point of automated translation.
Correct: it tells the model the rules and verifies them, which is cheap and effective.
A higher temperature makes outputs more varied, which makes consistency worse.
Word-by-word translation produces unnatural, often wrong sentences.
questions.explanation: Consistency problems usually come from the model not knowing which terms are fixed. A glossary of protected and preferred terms, plus an automatic check, makes the output consistent without changing the rest of the translation. It is cheap and easy to update as new brands appear.
questions.interview_tip: For AI quality issues, interviewers like the simplest fix that controls the problem and can be checked automatically.

questions.concept: Storing money as integer minor units instead of floats
questions.question: A payments team stores order amounts as floating-point rupees (e.g., 199.99). Finance finds reconciliation is off by a few paise across millions of orders. What's the standard fix?
options: Use double-precision floating-point numbers instead of single-precision ones
Run a nightly job that adjusts the totals so they match the bank's records
Round every amount to two decimal places just before it is shown to the user
Store amounts as whole numbers in the smallest unit (paise) or use a fixed-point decimal type
rationales: Double precision reduces the error but doesn't remove it; decimals still aren't exact.
Adjusting totals hides the problem and makes audits harder; it doesn't fix the cause.
Rounding only at display time hides the error but leaves stored values and totals wrong.
Correct: integers or decimal types represent money exactly, so no errors build up.
questions.explanation: Floating-point numbers can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so tiny errors add up across many transactions. Storing whole paise (19,999 instead of 199.99) or using a decimal type keeps money exact. This is standard practice in payment systems.
questions.interview_tip: Technical questions like this test whether you know the common traps. Explaining why floats fail for money signals good technical fluency.

questions.concept: Byte-based length limits truncating Indic-script text
questions.question: Your app limits usernames to 20 characters. Hindi and Tamil users say their names get cut off after about six characters, while English names fit. The backend measures length as the number of bytes in the UTF-8 string. What's happening?
options: Indic keyboards add hidden spaces between letters, which use up the character limit
Indic-script fonts are wider, so the text box can show fewer characters before it fills up
The database rejects non-Latin characters and silently cuts off the rest of the name
Devanagari and Tamil characters take 3 bytes each in UTF-8, so a byte limit cuts them early; limits should count visible characters
rationales: Indic keyboards don't insert hidden spaces; the issue is how bytes are counted.
Display width affects how text looks, not where the backend cuts it.
If the database rejected these characters, names wouldn't be stored at all, not neatly cut at six.
Correct: it explains the 20 ÷ 3 ≈ 6 pattern and points to the right fix.
questions.explanation: UTF-8 uses 1 byte for English letters but 3 bytes for each Devanagari or Tamil code point, so 20 bytes holds only about six. A visible letter can also combine several code points (a consonant plus a vowel sign). Length limits shown to users should count what users see as characters (grapheme clusters).
questions.interview_tip: For products serving Indian or global users, interviewers value awareness of how text encoding affects users. Linking a technical detail to a visible user problem is the key skill.

questions.concept: Setting free-trial length from time-to-value
questions.question: A project-management SaaS offers a 30-day free trial. Most users who convert reach their 'aha' moment (inviting three teammates and completing a task) within five days. 70% of trial users are inactive after day 10. What should the team test?
options: Keeping the 30 days but sending a reminder email every day from day 10 onward
A 60-day trial so that inactive users have more time to come back and try again
A shorter trial, such as 14 days, with onboarding focused on reaching the aha moment quickly
Removing the trial and asking every new user for a card before they can start
rationales: Daily emails to inactive users cause fatigue and unsubscribes without fixing the cause.
A longer trial extends the inactive period; most users who don't engage early won't come back.
Correct: it matches trial length to time-to-value and adds urgency, framed as a test.
Requiring a card is a much bigger change that cuts trial starts; it doesn't address the timing gap.
questions.explanation: Trial length should fit how long it takes to experience value. If value arrives in days, a long trial mostly adds a quiet period where users forget about the product. A shorter trial creates urgency and can raise conversion, as long as onboarding gets users to the aha moment fast. It should be tested, not assumed.
questions.interview_tip: Growth interviewers want you to tie levers like trial length to user behaviour data. Proposing a test rather than a final answer shows good judgment.

questions.concept: GPT-6.2 Astra launched in ChatGPT Work and Codex but not regular chat (Nov 2026)
questions.question: On 17 November 2026, OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. They were made available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for paid plans, but not in regular ChatGPT chat. Astra's API price is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra. From a PM's point of view, what does the choice of surfaces most plausibly signal?
options: The models are weaker at casual chat, so OpenAI is keeping them away from everyday users
The models are aimed at long, work-focused tasks, where paying users get the most value from expensive compute
Regulators blocked consumer use of the models in several markets, forcing a work-only launch
OpenAI is pulling back from developers, since API access is now a lower priority than apps
rationales: Nothing in the launch says the models are worse at chat; this is an unsupported guess.
Correct: it fits the facts (paid, work-focused surfaces) and the economics of expensive models.
There's no report of regulators blocking these models; inventing a cause isn't good analysis.
The API launched at the same time with a 20% price cut, which signals the opposite of pulling back.
questions.explanation: Launching a frontier model in work and coding surfaces puts expensive capacity where tasks are long, high-value and paid for. That's a common way to manage cost and capacity while showing the model's strengths. The source doesn't give OpenAI's stated reasoning, so this is the product logic, not a confirmed motive.
questions.interview_tip: When discussing current events, separate what was announced from what you infer. Interviewers value candidates who reason from facts about surfaces, pricing and cost, and say clearly what is inference.
